business_question: Does Microsoft's dependency on enterprise IT spending create hidden exposure to Federal Reserve interest rate policy?
description: Microsoft derives approximately 60% of its revenue from enterprise and commercial customers through Azure cloud services, Microsoft 365, and Dynamics. Enterprise IT budgets are macro-sensitive: during rate tightening cycles, corporate borrowing costs rise, capital allocation shifts away from discretionary technology investments, and IT spending growth slows. An investor holding Microsoft may view it as a defensive, rate-insensitive technology company — when in fact its commercial revenue base creates an indirect but measurable sensitivity to Federal Reserve policy.
future_expansion: Add Azure AI capex financing as a direct debt-sensitivity path (higher confidence when capex data is Level A)

evidence: Microsoft FY2024 Annual Report: Commercial cloud revenue $135bn representing ~60% of total revenue
Goldman Sachs Technology Research 2023: Enterprise IT spending growth shows 0.6 correlation with Fed Funds rate movements over 5-year cycles
Microsoft FY2024 Annual Report: Microsoft 365 Commercial, Azure, and Dynamics revenue dependent on enterprise budget cycles
IMF World Economic Outlook 2023: Rate tightening episodes reduce business investment by 3-5% on average within 12 months
Gartner IT Spending Forecast 2024: Enterprise software growth moderates during high-rate environments as CIOs defer discretionary spend
notes: Confidence [0.66, 0.70] reflects the indirect nature of this exposure.
